transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-29
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Sophie Lang (Arbor Health, Eng Lead), Marcus Reed (Arbor Health, CTO), Aisha Patel (Arbor Health, DevOps)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text generation streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, max_tokens, stop), retry/backoff strategies, and a short console handoff showing Optimize suggestions and cost breakdown. Customer wanted clarification on latency vs cost tradeoffs and how Redwood handles graceful degradation (fallbacks to smaller variants).

Topics covered:
- Streaming chunk semantics and partial tokens
- Idempotency and request dedupe for retries
- Retry/backoff best practices (exponential jitter + model fallback)
- Console: per-route latency/cost dashboards and Optimize recommendations (batching, quantization)
- Short troubleshooting lab: simulate 502 and walk through fallback policy + client retry flow
Action items in call (verbal): Maya to share security pack and recording; Diego to run bench; Aisha to provide traffic profile.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): ok good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, i run the AE motion for this region. Diego is our solutions engineer. Today we'll do a short demo of the hosted chat stream, show some console tips and then a quick lab on retries and fallback. Sound good?
[00:14] Sophie (Arbor Health): yep that sounds great. we want to understand latency behavior and what happens if the API returns errors under load. also curious about cost impacts.
[00:24] Diego (Redwood SE): awesome. i'll start by showing a simple streaming session and point out where the runtime emits partial tokens. so in streaming you get chunks, each chunk is a partial piece of the generation. clients should append and render progressively. i'll pull up the console now.
[00:40] [screen share noise] Diego: okay console, top-left you can see the per-route dashboard. this route is our chat-gen default. you can see median latency, p95 and token-cost breakdown. for customers like you, we recommend tracking median for UX and p95 for SLOs.
[01:05] Marcus (CTO): when you say token-cost breakdown, is that per-request or aggregated? curious how it maps to our billing windows.
[01:12] Diego: it's aggregated by time window but you can slice by token type (prompt vs completion). console also shows per-token USD estimates if you turn on cost-metrics. that helps you see the regen-heavy prompts driving cost.
[01:30] Sophie: ok can you show the streaming behavior with an actual sample prompt? we want to see partials and the abort / resume semantics.
[01:38] Diego: sure. i'll run a live call. curl -s -N -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"model":"redwood-large-1","input":"Summarize the latest clinical notes for patient 238","stream":true}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -> you'll see chunked events.
[02:05] [typing sound] Diego: there we go, first chunk arrives at ~120ms, subsequent chunks show steady token throughput. note that at 512 max_tokens the last chunk completes.
[02:22] Marcus: the ~120ms, is that cold start or already warmed? our concern is worst-case latency under heavy concurrency.
[02:30] Diego: good question. that's a warm path, cold start for a model variant can add ~100-300ms depending on KV cache state. but for sustained traffic we keep workers warm and use prefix caching to reduce per-token time.
[02:50] Sophie: you mentioned KV cache... we've seen docs reference 'KV cache' - can you explain in plain terms? i think our infra folks called it K-V cash last time (laughs).
[02:58] Diego: yeah, sometimes transcripts mis-hew -- kv cache stores prior activations for a session so generation doesn't re-compute large chunks on each step, it speeds up autoregressive decoding. it matters for long conversations.
[03:15] Maya: let's pivot to retries and fallbacks. Sophie, Marcus, what are your SLOs? p95 < 500ms? or lower?
[03:24] Sophie: ideally p95 under 700ms for chat in our clinician UI. cost target is... we don't want costs to double when we ramp.
[03:32] Maya: fair. for that SLO we usually recommend a two-pronged approach: client-side retry with idempotency key + exponential backoff with jitter, and server-side fallback policy.
[03:45] Diego: here's a typical flow: client sends request with idempotency key; on 5xx or transient network error, client retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff (retry intervals 200ms -> 600ms -> 1800ms, add jitter). if backend is under pressure we can route to a compatible smaller variant (redwood-medium-1) automatically. that reduces latency and cost.
[04:10] Marcus: if you fallback to a smaller variant, do we get different outputs/quality? how do you measure regressions?
[04:17] Diego: yes there can be quality delta. Redwood Optimize in the console can run cheap evals on a holdout promptset and give a quality vs latency chart so you can pick a variant threshold (e.g., fallback only for non-critical endpoints).
[04:35] Sophie: will that show examples where answers diverge?
[04:38] Diego: it surfaces aggregate metrics and sample outputs flagged for manual review. you can also pin model versions per route for strictness.
[04:48] [crosstalk] Aisha (DevOps): how do we capture and correlate errors for auditing? we need audit logs and request traces.
[04:56] Maya: console emits request traces with token-level timing. for Private or Dedicated we also integrate with your SIEM via syslog and we have KMS-integrations for encryption. we'll include that in the security pack.
[05:10] Diego: quick note on idempotency — for streaming, idempotency semantics are tricky because partials may have been received before retry. we recommend checkpointing at semantic boundaries (e.g. message IDs) and making the client resilient to duplicate partials.
[05:30] Sophie: can you simulate an error and show a retry + fallback in action? we'd like to see how the client behaves and what logs look like.
[05:38] Diego: yeah let's do a lab. i'll throttle the route in the console to trigger 502s. please watch the request trace.
[05:50] [screen share: console - throttling toggled] Diego: ok i've enabled a synthetic error injection policy at 10% sample for this route. now I'll run a small script that posts with an idempotency key and retries.
[06:10] [demo noise] Diego: first attempt got a 502 at ~130ms, client retried after 250ms, second attempt hit fallback route which is redwood-medium-1 and returned at ~350ms. console trace shows the original error and then the successful fallback.
[06:30] Marcus: can we see the trace for that sequence?
[06:33] Diego: yes, here's the trace, you can see request id, attempt numbers, and which model variant served. the trace includes approximate token timings, but partials for the failed attempt will be marked as incomplete.
[06:50] Sophie: is there a recommended backoff algorithm you've tested? exponential with full jitter?
[06:56] Diego: full jitter is what we recommend. a simple implementation: sleep = random(0, base * 2^attempt). base 200ms works for chat UI. avoid tight loops. also, implement a circuit-breaker so client pauses retries after sustained errors.
[07:12] Maya: i'll also point out that Redwood's smart routing can do capacity-tier fallback so traffic can go to a lower-cost region or a dedicated pool if host is overloaded. you can configure policies in the console.
[07:26] Aisha: what about idempotency storage? do you rely on us to persist keys, or do you provide a dedupe window?
[07:33] Diego: we accept idempotency keys and dedupe server-side for a configurable window (default 5 minutes). for long-lived workflows we suggest you persist keys client-side as well.
[07:45] Sophie: can we get an example payload that you recommend for chat streaming retries?
[07:50] Diego: sure, i read a trimmed example: POST /v1/chat with headers Authorization + Idempotency-Key. body: {"model":"redwood-large-1","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"..."}],"stream":true}. On the client, open SSE or http2 stream, and if you get a 502 mid-stream, close the stream and retry with same key. the service will either resume from checkpoint or return full generation depending on the checkpoint semantics.
[08:20] Sophie: resume semantics sound tricky. is it deterministic?
[08:24] Diego: not always. resume depends on what the backend persisted. for strict resume guarantees use small chunking or sequence numbers so client-side can reconcile duplicates.
[08:35] Marcus: switching topics: cost. you mentioned Optimize recommendations - can you show a real example where batching or quantization gave a big win?
[08:45] Diego: yes, in the console Optimize tab we ran a profiling job against an order-fulfillment promptset for a customer. By enabling batching at the route level and switching to an int8 quantized variant for non-critical endpoints, they reduced completion cost by ~35% while increasing median latency by ~60ms which stayed within their SLO.
[09:10] Sophie: interesting. do we need to change model code to accept quantized variants? or is it transparent?
[09:16] Diego: transparent to the API. you pick a quantization profile in the model catalog and Redwood handles runtime selection and kernel tuning. the caveat is potential small quality delta — Optimize shows the delta so you can make an informed choice.
[09:30] Aisha: any notes about caching and stale token concerns if we enable aggressive batching?
[09:36] Diego: batching aggregates multiple independent requests to amortize GPU work. it shouldn't change content for independent requests. if you rely on low-latency single-user interactions, set batch windows small (5-10ms). Optimize suggests batch windows based on your traffic.
[09:52] [pause] Maya: quick check — are there any compliance blockers we should know about? data residency?
[09:58] Marcus: for us PHI is sensitive, so we need private deployment or strong BCAs.
[10:04] Maya: noted. Private/ Dedicated are options; for Hosted we offer data controls, retention policies, and contractual clauses but for PHI we often recommend Private or on-prem. we'll include architecture notes in the security pack.
[10:18] Sophie: perfect. can you show how to enable per-route fallback policies in the console?
[10:22] Diego: sure. navigate to Routes -> select route -> Fallbacks. here you can add a policy: conditions (error rate, p95 latency threshold), action (route to variant or to dedicated pool), and cooldown. i'll demo adding one: error_rate > 5% over 1m -> fallback to redwood-medium-1 with cooldown 5m.
[10:48] [demo clicks] Diego: policy saved. now if the route crosses threshold traffic will be auto-routed. logs will show policy triggers.
[10:58] Aisha: if fallback triggers, do we get alerted via Slack or PagerDuty?
[11:02] Diego: yes, you can attach notifications to rollout policies. console supports Slack, PagerDuty, and webhook alerting.
[11:10] Marcus: let's return to the lab. can you pull the console trace and the raw request headers for the failed attempt, so our security folks can see that no sensitive payloads are logged?
[11:20] Diego: pulling trace now. note the console scrubs sensitive fields in logs by default—payload bodies are redacted unless you enable request-body retention for debugging.
[11:34] Sophie: good to know. can we record the session?
[11:37] Maya: yes we'll share the recording and the console export.
[11:42] Diego: ok for the lab, i'm going to run a mini-load test: 50 concurrent chat sessions using our sample script, with 10% error injection still on. watching traces...
[11:58] [load test noise] Diego: we're seeing the error injection cause retries; the fallback policy is triggering around minute 2 and routing ~18% of requests to medium variant. median latency is 240ms, p95 ~680ms under the synthetic load.
[12:22] Marcus: can you export the CSV? we want to correlate with our monitoring.
[12:26] Diego: csv exported and i'll attach in the follow-up.
[12:32] Sophie: you mentioned idempotency windows earlier. if we keep a 5 minute dedupe window server-side, could that cause accidental dedupe when a user legitimately retries after 6 minutes?
[12:40] Diego: after the dedupe window ends the key will no longer dedupe. pick windows aligned to your client behavior. for long-running jobs use separate jobs API with explicit job ids.
[12:52] Aisha: any limits on idempotency key length or format?
[12:55] Diego: we recommend UUIDv4 or similar — limit 128 bytes. we also sign keys server-side for anti-replay.
[13:04] Maya: wrapping up, high level recap — client retries with idempotency + exponential jitter, server-side fallback policies to smaller variants, console Optimize for batch/quantization suggestions, and security pack for PHI. action items: we'll share SOC2 + recording; Diego will run bench and share CSV; Aisha will provide traffic profile.
[13:26] Sophie: thanks. quick question — for the pilot, what does cost look like for a week of dedicated reserved capacity?
[13:33] Maya: i'll send a pilot quote. typical pilot is a 1-week reserved pool sized to your peak qps; pricing depends on GPU type. i'll include a cost sensitivity table in the follow-up.
[13:44] Marcus: any final blockers?
[13:46] Aisha: none from my side, just need to review security docs.
[13:50] Maya: perfect, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the security pack and the bench results.
[13:58] [meeting ends early — notes: customers asked for explicit resume semantics doc; include that in follow-up]
